clue.text: Standard of wine drunk with journalist, eating a new sort of cheese

parts.note: red is a colour, and so a kind, of wine

indicators.note: drunk means the word with staggers into a new order
eating means the journalist's letters swallow the next piece

parts.note: ED, short for editor, is the crossword journalist
blue is a type of veined cheese such as Stilton

explanation.surface: A wine-soaked hack munches on a novel cheese while a flag flies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' scrambles the clue's 'with'; 'eating' has the journalist swallow 'a new'. 'Standard' is a flag, not a level.
explanation.definitionFit: A standard is a flag, and the Union Jack, like the Stars and Stripes, is known by its three colours.

clue.text: Sees enough and rages about cause of climate change?

indicators.note: about here means turned round and scattered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who has seen enough of the climate crisis and rants about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbon dioxide and methane trap heat in the atmosphere, driving global warming; the question mark flags an example.

clue.text: Experts to include one into chopped ham

indicators.note: include means the first letters wrap around the following piece

parts.note: pros are professionals, experts

indicators.note: into means the one goes inside the word for chopped

parts.note: chopped means cut
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Specialists tell you to add something to diced ham.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nested containers: 'into' puts the one in the chopped word, and 'include' sets that whole piece between the experts and 'to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosciutto is Italian dry-cured ham, usually sliced very thin.

clue.text: Flying past in pick-up truck, towards Albany from New York?

indicators.note: in means the shuffled letters sit inside the truck's word

parts.note: a ute, short for utility vehicle, is an Australian pick-up truck

indicators.note: flying means the letters of past are sent off in a new order

explanation.surface: Speeding by in a pickup on the road north from New York City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flying' shuffles PAST into PSTA, which goes 'in' UTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Albany, the state capital, lies north of New York City, in the part of the state New Yorkers call the northern hinterland, so one heads that way.

clue.text: Scottish group just started live set in prison

indicators.note: set in means that letter is placed inside the word for prison

parts.note: the can is slang for prison

indicators.note: just started means only the opening letter of live is used

explanation.surface: A Highland family has only just begun life behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set in' puts L, the first of 'live', inside CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish clan is a kinship group sharing a surname and chief, like the MacDonalds.

clue.text: Limit on skill shown by ex-PM as a gardener

indicators.note: on means the limit sits above the next piece in this down entry

parts.note: a cap is an upper limit
ability means skill
Gordon Brown was UK Prime Minister 2007-10

explanation.surface: A former prime minister shows limited skill when tackling the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Brown was the British Prime Minister from 2007 to 2010.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancelot 'Capability' Brown was the great 18th-century English landscape designer of country-house parks.

clue.text: Chicken sandwich, US style? That'll get one animated

parts.note: yellow means cowardly, chicken
in America a long filled roll is a submarine, or sub, sandwich

explanation.surface: Ordering an American chicken sub might cheer one up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' looks like a filling, but it is the adjective meaning cowardly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beatles' 1968 film of that name is an animated cartoon, so it literally makes a story animated.

clue.text: Small show of joy perhaps, after rent reduction

parts.note: a rent is a tear or rip
a drop is a reduction, as in a price drop

explanation.surface: A tenant is mildly pleased when the rent comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' is the noun meaning a rip, not a payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Tears of joy are shed when happy, so a single one is a small display of delight; 'perhaps' marks the example.

clue.text: No 1 from Adele, originally by Queen

indicators.note: originally signals these letters must be put back into some other, original order

parts.note: R, for Regina, is the abbreviation for a queen

explanation.surface: A chart-topping single from the singer Adele, first released through Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' rearranges ADELE to LEADE; R (Regina) is the Queen, placed 'by' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Number one means the person at the head, the chief or top dog.

clue.text: Strokes, the first of which produces 8s

parts.note: which points back to the answer; its first letter is S
8 across is a drop of the eye's salt water, so someone who sheds them weeps

explanation.surface: A set of brushstrokes, the first of which yields sorrowful drops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which' refers to the answer itself: its first letter, S, followed by a word for crying.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeps are long smooth movements, as of a brush or oar, so they are strokes.

clue.text: Can't foul in the box, one might be feeling

indicators.note: in means the jumbled letters sit inside the television word

parts.note: the box is slang for television, the tele

indicators.note: foul means the letters of the word are messed up into a new order

explanation.surface: A footballer can't commit a foul in the penalty area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foul' shuffles CANT to NTAC, put 'in' TELE; 'the box' is British slang for television.
explanation.definitionFit: An octopus or snail's arm is a feeler, a limb used for touching and sensing, so it is something that feels.

clue.text: A little child is half-price fare

indicators.note: A little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A small child travels at half the adult fare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fare' looks like a ticket price, but here it means food.
explanation.definitionFit: Fare means food served, and a dish is a prepared item of food.

clue.text: Football team's about to struggle with questions after final whistle?

indicators.note: about means the team's letters surround the next pieces

parts.note: Inter Milan is a famous football club, Inter, with the 's kept
to vie is to struggle or compete

explanation.surface: A football club must deal with media grilling once the match ends.
explanation.walkthrough: Inter Milan is the Italian club; 'about' wraps the team's name, apostrophe-S included, round the struggle and the with.
explanation.definitionFit: Managers and players face reporters' questions straight after a match; the question mark marks this as one example of such sessions.

clue.text: Bad pun initially causes extreme anger or disgust

indicators.note: bad means the letters are spoilt and set in a new order
initially means only the first letter of causes is taken

parts.note: to enrage is to fill with extreme anger

explanation.surface: A dreadful pun first provokes fury, then revulsion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges PUN, C (from 'initially causes') and ENRAGE together; 'or' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Repugnance is strong distaste or revulsion, the feeling of disgust.

clue.text: Duel? Pot shot happened just before!

indicators.note: shot means wrecked or broken up, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A duel in which a pot shot was fired just before.
explanation.definitionFit: Events that led up to something preceded it and paved the way, coming immediately beforehand.

clue.text: Best work is before setter's filled stomach

indicators.note: before means the work comes first in the answer

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work

indicators.note: filled means the setter's word goes inside the stomach word

parts.note: tum is an informal word for stomach
the setter speaking is I; setter's means setter is, so I'M

explanation.surface: The ideal piece of work is one done after the setter has eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords the setter refers to themself as 'I', so 'setter's' is 'setter is'; 'filled' places that inside the stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: The optimum is the most favourable or ideal outcome, the best possible.

clue.text: Complaint, as Charlie Parker hurriedly withdrew broadcast

parts.note: the jazz saxophonist Charlie Parker was nicknamed Bird

indicators.note: broadcast means the word is heard rather than read, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: flew means fled, left in haste

explanation.surface: Charlie Parker hastily pulled out of a radio broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broadcast' turns FLEW into its same-sounding FLU.
explanation.definitionFit: Complaint is a word for an illness, and avian influenza is a disease.

clue.text: Tabloid outing 9? Pretty inappropriate

indicators.note: outing means put out, removing the letter named

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
9 across means number one, read here as the first letter, S
becoming means attractive, pretty

explanation.surface: A tabloid outing the newspaper's chief: pretty improper behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid; 'outing' its first letter (the 9 across, read literally) leaves UN.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbecoming conduct is improper or unsuitable, not fitting for someone's position.

clue.text: Trek round with openers from Middlesex, promptly after close of play

indicators.note: close of means the final letter of play is taken

parts.note: a round thing is shaped like O

indicators.note: openers from means first letters of Middlesex and promptly

explanation.surface: A cricket report: Middlesex openers walk out promptly after stumps.
explanation.walkthrough: Middlesex is an English county cricket side; 'after' puts the close of play first.
explanation.definitionFit: Yomp is British military slang for a long laden march, a trek over rough ground.

clue.text: Got into bed with a novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are arranged in a fresh way

explanation.surface: Someone climbed into bed with a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book, but signals a rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Got and obtained are synonyms meaning acquired.

clue.text: Shipbuilder dropping into Bath regularly

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter, here the second, fourth and so on

explanation.surface: A boatwright pops into Bath from time to time.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Noah built the ark to save his family and the animals from the flood.

clue.text: Those drying Sierra winds?

indicators.note: winds means twists round, so the letters are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: Mountain winds that dry the land.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes horses and racks for drying laundry are things that dry washing.

clue.text: 'Aha!', said solver, 'A stinker!'

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the words are a sound-alike for the entry

parts.note: the solver is you, addressed by the setter, and a reeker is something that reeks, a stinker: together you reeker

explanation.surface: A solver cries out on cracking a stinker of a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A stinker' looks like a hard puzzle; it is a smelly person.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes' cry of discovery is the classic exclamation of sudden triumphant realisation.

clue.text: Delicate six-footer in league champion side

parts.note: an ace is a champion, a top performer
a wing is a side, as of a building or a team

explanation.surface: A star winger in a top league side with a fine touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'six-footer' is not a tall player but an insect, which has six legs.
explanation.definitionFit: This green insect has delicate, lacy, veined wings, and as an insect it has six legs.
